summary: Designed for the NASA space apps challenge 2026, we developed an interactive website which takes images from the SPHEREx telescope and sends it out to the general public in an easily accessible way to make it possible for anyone to make discoveries. We implemented this with various features to search and generate randomized or targeted coordinates in the sky included afterwards with multiple tools to make it easier for people to enhance the differences between multiple images of the same spot of sky. This can not just save NASA time combing through every single piece of information themselves, it transforms the way satellite images are processed altogether by making it so easy for anyone, even people who don’t know much about image processing or astronomy to find information. This revolutionizes the entire way us astronomers process information and makes it so much easier and more public.
details:
Our project, SPHEREx Infrared Sky Explorer (SPHEREx SkyView), is an interactive web platform that transforms raw near-infrared data from NASA’s SPHEREx mission into a visual, color-layered discovery tool for the general public. Designed so anyone can explore invisible wavelengths without needing an astronomy or image-processing background, the dark-mode interface tracks mission metrics (6 Detector Arrays, 102 Spectral Channels, and Visited Fields) and lets users query specific J2000 coordinates, select benchmark targets, or generate randomized all-sky and unvisited pointings. Once a sky region is selected, the results page displays seven distinct views: six individual detector bands spanning 0.75 to 5.0 microns alongside a seventh full-spectrum composite image. Interactive RGB sliders, two-color pairing controls, and customizable opacity layering allow users to isolate subtle details and compare different observations, while an integrated color-translation guide decodes what each infrared wavelength reveals about chemical makeup—helping everyday users identify water, hydrogen, carbon dioxide, and carbon monoxide. Below the viewer, a timeline scroll bar, slideshow, and timelapse generator complete with date, time, and coordinate metadata let users track moving objects and brightness shifts over time.

By turning complex 102-band infrared spectrometry into an intuitive color-mixing and layering experience, our platform lowers the barrier to citizen science and scales discovery across SPHEREx’s massive all-sky survey so astronomers do not have to sift through over a billion objects alone. We built the web application using modern frontend web technologies alongside NASA/IPAC IRSA data specifications, and we utilized Google Gemini during development to accelerate prototyping, generate and debug code, and structure our multi-band color-mixing and coordinate-querying logic. Regarding testing and data constraints, while the challenge recommended benchmarking against specific targets like Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, and WISE 0855, complete multi-epoch SPHEREx image cutouts for those exact coordinates were not yet available in the public archive during our build window. To solve this, we included direct quick-select presets for those benchmark targets on our home page and validated our visualization, color-layering, and timelapse tools using available sample data—ensuring our pipeline is fully ready to display real observations of Barnard’s Star and other targets as soon as NASA releases those sky patches.
